title: UC Berkeley Compound Cuts Weight 18% in Mice Without Suppressing Appetite
excerpt: An oral molecule called TOFA boosted energy expenditure and preserved muscle mass in obese mice, offering a potential complement to GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic.
body:
• UC Berkeley researchers found that an oral compound called TOFA reduced body weight by 18% in obese mice over four weeks without suppressing appetite or causing significant muscle loss.
  • Unlike GLP-1 drugs such as Ozempic and Wegovy, TOFA works by boosting energy expenditure — the mice burned up to 18% more energy with no change in food intake or physical activity.
  • TOFA also improved insulin sensitivity, glucose control, and fatty liver markers, and did not raise triglycerides like other compounds in its class.
  • The compound showed additive or synergistic effects when combined with GLP-1 drugs in mouse models, suggesting potential as a complementary therapy.

Researchers at the University of California, Berkeley have identified an oral compound that produced substantial weight loss in obese mice through a mechanism fundamentally different from the GLP-1 drugs that dominate the market. The molecule, known as TOFA (5-tetradecyloxy-2-furoic acid), reduced body weight by an average of 18% over four weeks without changing how much the animals ate — and without significant loss of lean muscle mass.

The study, published in the journal Science Advances on August 21, comes as millions of patients worldwide take injectable medications like semaglutide (Ozempic, Wegovy) and tirzepatide (Mounjaro, Zepbound) for weight loss. Those drugs work primarily by suppressing appetite, but some users experience gastrointestinal side effects, nutritional deficiencies, and loss of muscle mass that can lead to frailty over time.

A Different Metabolic Lever

TOFA takes a different approach. Instead of reducing calorie intake, it increases the body's energy expenditure — how many calories the body burns.

"Body weight responds to two levers: taking in fewer calories, or spending more energy. GLP-1s work almost entirely on the first, so we went after the second."

— Anders Näär, Professor of Metabolic Biology and Nutrition, UC Berkeley

In the study, obese mice were fed a high-fat diet until they developed obesity, then received TOFA orally twice daily for four weeks. Food intake remained unchanged, physical activity did not increase, and body temperature stayed stable — yet whole-body energy expenditure rose by as much as 18%, according to senior author Anders Näär.

The compound works through a dual mechanism. It belongs to a class called ACC inhibitors, which block enzymes involved in producing lipids such as cholesterol and triglycerides. But the researchers found TOFA also activates cellular receptors called PPARα and PPARδ, which switch on genes that help cells absorb and burn fat for energy. This coordinated response appears to be why TOFA avoids a problem that has derailed other ACC inhibitors in clinical trials: raising triglyceride levels, which poses cardiovascular risks.

Muscle Preservation Sets It Apart

Preserving lean muscle mass during weight loss remains one of the most significant clinical challenges in obesity treatment. GLP-1 drugs, by reducing food intake broadly, can cause patients to lose muscle along with fat — a particular concern for older adults and those at risk of frailty.

In the Berkeley study, most of the weight the mice lost came from body fat, while muscle and other lean tissues were largely preserved. The researchers note this is consistent with TOFA's mechanism: it targets energy expenditure rather than food restriction, so the body continues to receive the protein and nutrients muscles need.

Potential as a Complement to GLP-1s

The researchers also tested whether TOFA could work alongside existing GLP-1 medications. In mouse experiments combining TOFA with semaglutide and tirzepatide, they found greater improvements in body weight, glucose control, insulin levels, and triglycerides than either treatment alone.

"In our combination experiments, TOFA worked additively or synergistically with the GLP-1 appetite-suppressing drugs, so we view it as complementary rather than as a replacement," Näär said.

Interestingly, when researchers tried giving mice two separate compounds — one to block lipid production and a second to boost energy expenditure — the combination was less effective than TOFA alone. This suggests the molecule's dual action within cells produces a coordinated metabolic response that single-target approaches cannot replicate.

From the 1970s Lab to a Biotech Startup

TOFA was first discovered in the 1970s as part of early research into ACC inhibitors. Several compounds in this class reached mid-stage clinical trials over the decades but none were approved for metabolic disease, largely because of the triglyceride problem. The Berkeley team's discovery that TOFA also activates fat-burning pathways — avoiding that side effect — has opened a new path forward.

The researchers have founded a company called ReRx Therapeutics, with support from Berkeley's SkyDeck accelerator, to carry the work toward human clinical trials. They caution that TOFA has only been studied in animals and its safety and efficacy in humans remain untested.

What This Means

For the growing number of people using or considering weight-loss medications — including a significant population in the Indian diaspora where diabetes and metabolic syndrome prevalence is elevated — TOFA represents a potentially complementary approach that addresses one of the biggest drawbacks of current treatments. Human trials will determine whether the mouse results translate, but the underlying science offers a credible new direction in obesity medicine.
